languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone who makes a serious mistake.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did the person do wrong, and what did they do next?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response may use “because ...”, “I will ... / I won’t ...”, “when ...”, “started + -ing”, “I don’t know what I should ...”, “showed ... the way to ...”, “worse/better than ...”, or “cannot ...”. Keep the sentences connected around one new situation rather than retelling Chapter 11.

feedback.correct: Keep the response coherent: Show the choice, the reaction, the uncertainty, and the next step.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what happened and why: “… because …”
discussionPrompts.example: Karim lost the money for the class trip because he left it on the bus.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Make a strong promise: “I will …” or “I won’t …”
discussionPrompts.example: He said to himself, “I won’t hide this from my teacher.”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Show they are not sure: “I don’t know what I should …”
discussionPrompts.example: But at first, he didn’t know what he should say to her.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say what they learned: “… guided him to …” or “… is better than …”
discussionPrompts.example: His older sister guided him to tell the truth, and he learned that honesty is better than hiding a mistake.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What happened to Qabil’s face?
options: It became red from the sun.
It became very dark with anger.
beforeYouRead.quote: Qabil’s face became very dark with anger

iCan: I can tell how the raven showed Qabil what to do.
I can make a firm promise with “will” or “won’t”.
I can write what someone should do after a serious mistake.

pages.title: The Legacy of Adam
pages.content: He went far away. Prophet Adam (pbuh) became very sad. He lost both of his sons on the same day. The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger. But as a prophet and the father of his other children, Adam (pbuh) had to continue his life. He got old over the years. His children and grandchildren moved to different parts of the world and spread his message worldwide. The message still calls upon people to turn away from Satan’s tricks and jealousy, to do good, and to avoid evil. It also teaches people the importance of admitting mistakes and turning back to Allah. Allah never left people alone. He sent His prophets, and their stories still guide us.

vocabulary.definition: Carried or passed something to many people or places.
Accepting or saying that something is true.
An important idea or teaching passed to others.
To show the right direction or way to act.

hotspots.title: A Family Across the World
hotspots.description: Adam (pbuh) continued his life, and his children and grandchildren spread across the world.

hotspots.title: A Lasting Message
hotspots.description: The message of Adam (pbuh) still teaches people to avoid jealousy, admit their mistakes and turn back to Allah.

exercises.title: Continuing After Loss
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 12.
exercises.question: Adam was very sad because he lost both of his sons on the same day. Why did he still have to continue his life?
options: Qabil came back home and asked his father to forgive him.
He was a prophet and the father of his other children.
Allah sent a raven to Adam to tell him what he had to do next.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12 says: “But as a prophet and the father of his other children, Adam (pbuh) had to continue his life.” Qabil “went far away,” and the raven belongs to Chapter 11.

feedback.correct: Yes. His duties as a prophet and a father helped him to go on with patience.
feedback.incorrect: Read the middle of Chapter 12. Find the sentence that starts with “But”.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Is This Sentence Doing?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 12. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger.” What does this sentence do?
options: It reports a rule that Adam gave to his sons.
It describes what true believers did on that day.
It says that anger is impossible to control.
It gives advice that the writer takes from the story.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “The story suggests that …” introduces an interpretation: A lesson the writer draws from the events, not an event itself. “Should + verb” gives advice about the right way to act. Together they turn the story of the two brothers into a recommendation for readers today.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Suggests that” gives the writer’s interpretation, and “should” gives advice.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the subject: “The story” suggests something. Is this an event in the story, or a lesson taken from it? What does “should” usually express?

languageFocusExercises.title: Necessity, Time and Continuity
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 12 with words from the bank. Three words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which word shows a need, which shows time passing, and which means “even now”?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: But as a prophet and the father of his other children, Adam (pbuh) [blank] continue his life. He got old [blank] the years. … He sent His prophets, and their stories [blank] guide us.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Had to” shows what was necessary in the past because of Adam’s role (as a prophet and a father). “Over the years” shows slow change across a long period. “Still” (before the main verb) shows that something continues now and has not stopped: the prophets’ stories guide us today.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed past necessity, change over time and continuity.
feedback.incorrect: Read Chapter 12 again. Is the first sentence about the past? Which word goes with “the years”? Which word shows that the guidance continues today?

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about the story’s message?

errorItems.sentence: It also teaches people the importance of admit mistakes and turning back to Allah.
… calls upon people to turn away from Satan’s tricks and jealousy, to do good, and avoiding evil.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: After a preposition such as “of”, use the -ing form, and keep both actions the same: “the importance of admitting … and turning back …”. In a list, the items should be parallel (the same form): “to turn away …, to do good, and to avoid evil”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You made the verb forms match in each sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the other verb in each list: “turning back” in the first sentence, and “to turn away … to do good” in the second. Make the wrong verb match them.

languageFocusExercises.title: A Lesson That Remains Useful
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone whose life teaches a useful lesson.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did the person do, and what can we learn?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response may use “As a/an ..., ... had to ...”, “over the years ...”, “still ...”, “never ...”, “the story/experience suggests that ... should ...”, or “the importance of + -ing”. Keep the four sentences connected around one new situation.

feedback.correct: Keep the response coherent: past role, development, continuing influence, and present lesson.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the role and a past duty: “As a …, she had to …”
discussionPrompts.example: As a young nurse, my grandmother had to work long nights in a small village clinic.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Show a change: “Over the years, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Over the years, she became an expert and trained many young nurses.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say what still matters now: “… still …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her kindness still influences the people in our village today.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give the lesson: “… shows the importance of + -ing” or “… suggests that we should …”
discussionPrompts.example: Her life shows the importance of helping others without waiting for thanks.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: According to the chapter, what still guides us today?
beforeYouRead.quote: He sent His prophets, and their stories still guide us.

iCan: I can explain the message Adam (pbuh) left for people.
I can say what still matters today.
I can share a useful lesson from someone’s life.

groupTask.title: Lessons That Still Guide Us

roles.name: Quote Finder
roles.job: You copy one lesson sentence from Chapter 12 exactly.

roles.name: Linker
roles.job: You find a sentence in an earlier chapter, such as Chapter 7 or Chapter 11, that shows the same lesson.

roles.name: Writer
roles.job: You explain the lesson and write two school examples.

roles.name: Designer and Presenter
roles.job: You make the poster or record the short audio clip and present it.

steps: Choose one lesson from Chapter 12: staying away from jealousy, controlling anger, admitting mistakes or doing good. For example: “The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger.”
Link it to an earlier chapter. For example, Chapter 7 says they “learned from their mistake and decided never to repeat it”.
Explain what the lesson means and give two realistic school examples. Use at least two patterns such as “decided never to …”, “the importance of + -ing” or “still”.
Make a one-page poster or a short audio clip in clear English. Nobody draws or acts as a person from the story; you only quote and explain the book.
groupTask.share: Each group shows its poster or plays its clip, reads its quote aloud and gives one school example.
groupTask.solo: Choose one lesson from Chapter 12, copy the sentence exactly, link it to Chapter 7 or 11 and write four sentences with two school examples.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your whole-book understanding with eight independent questions.

exercises.title: Adam and the Angels
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 2, Adam knew less than the angels, so the angels had to teach him.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2: “Later, He taught Adam (pbuh) everything he needed to do good on earth. He gave Adam (pbuh) more knowledge than the angels.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. Allah Himself taught Adam, and He gave him more knowledge than the angels.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the last paragraph of Chapter 2. Who taught Adam, and how did his knowledge compare with the angels’?

exercises.title: Life in Paradise
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: In Paradise, Adam and Eve had many rules to follow, so life there was difficult.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “All the blessings in Paradise were for them.” And: “Allah only asked them not to go near one tree.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. Paradise was full of blessings, and there was only one request: not to go near one tree.
feedback.incorrect: Reread Chapter 5. How many things did Allah ask Adam and Eve not to do?

exercises.title: After the Fruit
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 6.
exercises.question: How did Adam feel as soon as he finished eating the fruit?
options: He felt pain, sadness and shame in his heart.
He felt proud that he would never die now.
He felt angry with Eve for giving him the fruit.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “When Adam finished eating, he felt that his heart was filled with pain, sadness and shame. The surrounding atmosphere changed and the internal harmony ceased.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Adam knew at once that something was wrong: His heart was filled with pain, sadness and shame.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 6. What filled Adam’s heart? Also check who picked the fruit.

exercises.title: “I Am Shy of You”
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Allah asked, “Are you running away from Me?” What does Adam’s answer, “No, my Lord, but I am shy of You,” show?
options: He was afraid of punishment and wanted to hide from Allah.
He did not think he had done anything wrong in the garden.
He felt ashamed of his mistake but still turned to Allah.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: Adam “bowed down and cried, “Forgiveness! Forgiveness!”” He was not running away; he was ashamed of his mistake and asked Allah to pardon him.

feedback.correct: Well done. Adam’s shyness came from shame and respect. He did not run away; he bowed down and asked for forgiveness.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the first two paragraphs of Chapter 7. Did Adam run away, or did he ask for something?

exercises.title: Teaching the Children
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 9.
exercises.question: What did Adam (pbuh) and Eve teach their children?
options: to pray only to Allah and be aware of Iblis’s tricks
to leave their land one day and look for the way back to Paradise
to listen to Iblis because he knew many secrets of the garden
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “Adam (pbuh) and Eve taught their children to pray only to Allah and be aware of Iblis and his tricks because Iblis was their enemy, not their friend.”

feedback.correct: Correct. They taught their children to worship Allah alone and to be careful of Iblis because he was their enemy.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 9. What did Adam and Eve teach, and what did they say about Iblis?

exercises.title: Why an Offering?
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 10.
exercises.question: Why did Habil and Qabil have to make an offering to Allah?
options: They wanted to thank Allah for a good harvest.
Their father asked them to choose a new shepherd.
They needed to solve a serious disagreement.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10: “One day, they were in a serious disagreement. To solve the problem, they had to make an offering to Allah.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The offering was a way to settle their serious disagreement, and each brother’s choice showed his heart.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 10. What problem did the offering have to solve?

exercises.title: The Raven
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 11.
exercises.question: Qabil cried, “I am worse than this raven.” What does he mean?
options: The raven was stronger than him and could fight better.
The raven had taken the offering that Allah accepted.
Even a bird knew what to do, but he did not.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: the raven “showed Qabil the way to put his brother’s dead body in the pit.” Qabil said, “I cannot hide my brother’s dead body.”

feedback.correct: Well done. A bird had to show Qabil what to do. He felt small, helpless and full of regret.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the end of Chapter 11. What did the raven show Qabil, and what could he not do?

exercises.title: A Lasting Message
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to the last chapter, Adam’s message also teaches people to admit their mistakes and turn back to Allah.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “It also teaches people the importance of admitting mistakes and turning back to Allah.” This is exactly what Adam and Eve did in Chapter 7.

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The message repeats Adam’s own lesson: Admit the mistake and turn back to Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the end of Chapter 12. What does the message teach about mistakes?

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Consolidate grammar, discourse relationships, and communicative functions from across the chapters, then use them in new connected contexts.

exercises.title: Notice: Looking Back, Looking Forward, True Now
exercises.instructions: Looking back, looking ahead, or true now? Put each part in the right group.
exercises.question: Does it look back, look ahead, or say what is true now?

items: He said He had decided to place a ruler (khalifah) on earth.
… Allah had put him far from His help.
… they forgot the warning Allah had given them.

dragDropGroups.group: Looks forward: It was still ahead
items: … He told the angels that He was going to create a human.
They would direct, control and make everything better on the planet.
They would use land to grow crops and keep animals.
Arrogance is the biggest barrier …
We all come from their children.
… their stories still guide us.

Looks back: It happened earlier: He said He had decided to place a ruler (khalifah) on earth.
… Allah had put him far from His help.
… they forgot the warning Allah had given them.
Looks forward: It was still ahead: … He told the angels that He was going to create a human.
They would direct, control and make everything better on the planet.
They would use land to grow crops and keep animals.
True now, for the reader: We all come from their children.

exercises.explanation: In a story told in the past, every past moment is a point of view. Had + past participle (had decided, had put, had given) looks back from that moment to something that happened before it. Was going to / would + verb looks forward from that moment to something that was still in the future (the human, the work on earth). The present simple (is, are, guide) leaves the story and says what is true now, for us.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated looking back, looking forward and the present.
feedback.incorrect: Find the verb in each part. Is it had + past participle, would / was going to, or a present form (is, are, guide)? Compare Chapters 1, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 12.

exercises.title: Notice: Whose Idea Is It?
exercises.instructions: Read the two sentences. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 3: “Iblis thought that Adam was an unimportant being created from clay.” Chapter 12: “The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger.” What is the difference between “thought that” and “The story suggests that … should”?
options: Both report facts that the narrator agrees with, so the reader should accept them as true.
“Thought that” gives a character’s view, which may be wrong; “suggests that … should” gives advice that the writer takes from the story.
“Thought that” gives the narrator’s own judgment about Adam; “suggests that … should” reports Iblis’s exact words.
Both tell us exactly what a character said aloud, word for word, at that moment in the story.
exercises.explanation: Verbs such as thought that and believed tell us that an idea belongs to a character, and the idea can be wrong: In the same chapter the narrator says plainly, “Iblis was arrogant.” The story suggests that … introduces an interpretation, a lesson the writer draws from the events, and should turns it into advice for readers today.

feedback.correct: Correct. A reporting verb shows whose idea it is; “suggests that … should” marks the writer’s lesson.
feedback.incorrect: Ask who holds each idea: A character in the story, or the writer looking at the whole story? Compare Chapter 3 with the middle of Chapter 12.

exercises.title: Notice: Verbs That Shape the Story
exercises.instructions: Match each phrase from the book with its meaning.
exercises.question: What do continue, manage, decide and stop mean here?

matchingPairs.left: But Iblis continued saying he was right
matchingPairs.right: did not give up his claim

matchingPairs.left: Eventually, Iblis managed to trick them.
matchingPairs.right: succeeded in the end, after trying for some time
made a firm choice about the future
went on doing this, with no end

correctAnswer.But Iblis continued saying he was right: did not give up his claim
succeeded in the end, after trying for some time
correctAnswer.decided never to repeat it: made a firm choice about the future
correctAnswer.Allah never stopped sending messengers: went on doing this, with no end

exercises.explanation: The first verb changes the meaning of the action. Continue + -ing and never stop + -ing show that an action goes on without a break. Manage + to + verb means succeeding in something difficult, and eventually adds the idea of after some time. Decide (never) + to + verb gives a decision about the future. Notice that some verbs are followed by -ing and others by to + verb.

feedback.correct: Correct. You found how each verb shapes the action after it.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the first verb in each phrase: continued, managed, decided, never stopped. Does it show going on, success, or a decision?

exercises.title: Build: Reason, Contrast, Conclusion
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines from the book with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word gives a reason, shows a difference, or sums up?
exercises.fillBlanksText: He thought he was more important and more valuable than Adam (pbuh) [blank] he believed his origin was superior. … Adam was in Paradise, [blank] he started to feel lonely. … After a period of time, when a community formed, Adam (pbuh) became the first Messenger of Allah. [blank], he became the first human, the first father, and the first messenger of Islam. … Qabil didn’t care about pleasing Allah and his father Adam (pbuh). [blank], real goodness is giving out the best and the most loved.
exercises.explanation: “Because” + a full clause gives a reason: his belief about his origin. “Because of” would need a noun. “But” joins two ideas inside one sentence that do not fit together easily: Paradise, and yet loneliness. “Thus” starts a sentence that sums up what came before. “However” starts a new sentence that turns to a contrasting view: Qabil’s attitude against real goodness. “Although” needs a full clause after it and cannot stand alone with a comma.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked a reason, a contrast, a conclusion and a contrasting view.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Does the next part give a reason, a surprise inside the same sentence, a summary, or a new contrasting view? Check Chapters 3, 5, 9 and 10.

exercises.title: Build: What Follows the Verb?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: Which form comes after “convinced them”, “wanted people” and “barrier to”?

formChoices.sentence: He convinced them [choice] his lies, …
They wanted people [choice] Allah in their minds …
Arrogance is the biggest barrier to [choice] the right way …

exercises.explanation: Convince + person + to + verb and want + person + to + verb say what someone persuades or wants another person to do; English does not say want that they … . In a barrier to …, to is a preposition, not part of the verb, so it is followed by -ing, like “care about pleasing” and “the importance of admitting”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Person + to + verb after convince and want; a preposition + -ing.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the words before the gap. Is there a person after the verb (convinced them, wanted people)? Is to a preposition here (a barrier to …)? Check Chapters 6, 7 and 9.

exercises.title: Build: Fix the Comparison or the Tense
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
exercises.question: Can you fix the comparing words and the past verb?

errorItems.sentence: It was wonderfuller than we can imagine.
Qabil cried and said, “I am worst than this raven. …”
Prophet Adam (pbuh) became very sad. He has lost both of his sons on the same day.

exercises.explanation: Long adjectives such as “wonderful” make the comparative with more … than, not with -er. Bad – worse – worst: “worse than” compares two things, and “worst” is the superlative (“the worst thing in life”). The present perfect (has lost) does not go with a finished time in the past (on the same day); the story uses the past simple.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected both comparisons and the past verb.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Is it a comparison of two things (more … than, worse than)? Is the time finished (on the same day)? Compare with Chapters 5, 11 and 12.

exercises.title: Build: Report What They Said
exercises.instructions: Report what the people said. Write the missing words.
exercises.question: What changes when we report someone’s words?

transformItems.source: Iblis said, “I am better than Adam (pbuh). …”
transformItems.frame: Iblis said that he [blank] better than Adam (pbuh).

transformItems.source: When Habil heard this, he said, “I won’t fight back and harm you. …”
transformItems.frame: Habil told his brother that he [blank] fight back and harm him.

exercises.explanation: After a past reporting verb (said, told), the verb usually moves one step back: am → was, will not (won’t) → would not (wouldn’t). The pronouns change too because the narrator now speaks about the characters: I → he, you → him. Chapter 5 does the same: Iblis “whispered to them that if they ate from that one tree, they would never die.”

feedback.correct: Correct. am → was and won’t → wouldn’t when we report the words.
feedback.incorrect: Move the verb one step into the past: am → ?, won’t → ?. Then check the pronouns. Look again at Chapters 3 and 11.

exercises.title: Use: Our Garden Project
exercises.instructions: Complete this new text with words from the bank. Three words are extra.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words in a story about your school?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last autumn, our class decided to clean the old school garden. At first, it looked like an easy job, [blank] the garden was full of rubbish and dry leaves. For six weeks, we [blank] work there every Friday afternoon. Some students wanted to stop [blank] the weather was cold and windy. Our teacher told us that the younger pupils would play in the garden in spring. [blank] nobody gave up. In the end, we managed to plant twenty young trees, and the garden looked more beautiful than ever.
exercises.explanation: “But” joins the first picture (an easy job) and the reality (rubbish). “Had to” is past necessity; “must” is not used for the past. “Because” + a clause gives the reason (“because of” needs a noun). “That is why” points back to the teacher’s words and gives the result. The text also uses the book’s would (a future seen from the past), managed to and more … than.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new story.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each gap: A contrast, a past necessity, a reason, or a result? Is the next part a clause or a noun?

exercises.title: Use: Check New Sentences
exercises.instructions: Each new sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
exercises.question: Can you fix these new sentences about everyday life?

errorItems.sentence: When I arrived at the bus stop, the bus has already left.
Our teacher wanted us bringing our old books to the school library.
Our coach often talks about the importance of help each other.

exercises.explanation: The bus left before I arrived, so we look back with had + past participle: “had already left”. Want + person + to + verb: “wanted us to bring”. After a preposition such as “of”, use -ing: “the importance of helping each other”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s patterns correctly in new sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which action happened first? Is there a person after “wanted”? Is there a preposition before the verb?

exercises.title: Use: A Mistake Put Right
exercises.instructions: Write 5–6 sentences about a mistake you put right. Tell a partner first.
exercises.question: Can you tell a true story about a mistake you put right?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Last week, I had to bring my group’s poster to class. I forgot it because I was in a hurry. When I arrived at school, I realized that I had left it on my desk. It wasn’t on purpose, but my group was upset. However, I decided to tell my teacher the truth, and I managed to make a new poster at lunchtime. This experience suggests that we should admit our mistakes quickly; it shows the importance of saying sorry and putting things right.”

feedback.correct: Check your sentences: had to, because, had + past participle, but / however, decided (never) to, managed to, should, the importance of + -ing.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 1–2 — What happened and why: “Last …, I had to … . I … because … .”
discussionPrompts.example: Last month, I had to bring my part of a group poster for science class. I forgot it at home because I was busy with a football match.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Look back at the mistake: “I realized that I had … .” / “It wasn’t on purpose, but …”
discussionPrompts.example: I realized that I had let my group down: It wasn’t on purpose, but they had to wait for me.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — A better choice: “However, I decided (never) to … .” / “I managed to … .”
discussionPrompts.example: However, I decided never to leave my work until the last day, and I managed to finish my part the next morning.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — The lesson: “This experience suggests that we should … . It shows the importance of + -ing …”
discussionPrompts.example: This experience suggests that we should plan our work early. It shows the importance of keeping promises to our classmates.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Demonstrate whole-book mastery through ten independent B1 activities.

exercises.title: What the Story Is About
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 1 with one word: role, home or past.
exercises.question: What does Chapter 1 say the story has many messages about?
exercises.fillBlanksText: In this story, there are numerous important messages about humans’ [blank] in life.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “In this story, there are numerous important messages about humans’ role in life.” The same chapter explains that role: Allah “had decided to place a ruler (khalifah) on earth.”

feedback.correct: Yes. From the first chapter, the story is about the job and responsibility humans have in life.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of the first paragraph of Chapter 1. What is the story’s message about humans?

exercises.title: Colors and Value
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that connects the two chapters.
exercises.question: Chapter 2 explains why humans have different skin colors. How does the end of Chapter 3 build on this?
options: It says people with the same color should stay in one group.
It agrees with Iblis that the material of creation decides value.
It says color, race or group does not make anyone greater.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 2 says Allah shaped Adam from “soil from different parts of the earth”, and “That’s why humans have different skin colors.” Chapter 3 ends: “in the sight of Allah, superiority or greatness did not come from race, color, or being a member of a certain group.”

feedback.correct: Yes. All colors come from the same creation, so no color makes one person better than another, which is the mistake Iblis made about origin.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 3. What does it say about race and color?

exercises.title: Warned in Advance
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: Adam knew that Iblis was his enemy before Iblis came to him and Eve in Paradise.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 ends: “Allah told Adam (pbuh) that Iblis was his enemy and warned him to be careful of Iblis.” Only later, in Paradise, does Iblis come near them “pretending to be their friend”.

feedback.correct: True. Allah warned Adam first, so Iblis had to hide who he was and pretend to be a friend.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of Chapter 4, then the end of Chapter 5. Which comes first?

exercises.title: Iblis Step by Step
exercises.instructions: Match each moment with what Iblis did then.
exercises.question: How does Iblis act at each stage of the story?

matchingPairs.right: He refused to respect Adam because of his origin.
He waited for a chance to keep Adam from Allah’s kindness.
He came near Adam and Eve pretending to be their friend.
He stayed around because he wanted people not to remember Allah.

correctAnswer.In front of the angels: He refused to respect Adam because of his origin.
correctAnswer.After Allah sent him away: He waited for a chance to keep Adam from Allah’s kindness.
correctAnswer.In Paradise: He came near Adam and Eve pretending to be their friend.
correctAnswer.On earth: He stayed around because he wanted people not to remember Allah.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: Iblis did not respect Adam because “he believed his origin was superior.” Chapter 4: “He waited for a chance to keep Adam (pbuh) away from Allah’s kindness”. Chapter 5: “Iblis came near them pretending to be their friend.” Chapter 8: “He was still there because he wanted people not to remember Allah.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Iblis’s arrogance turns into hatred, then into a trick, and then into a plan that continues on earth.
feedback.incorrect: Follow Iblis through Chapters 3, 4, 5 and 8. What does he do in each place?

exercises.title: Not on Purpose
exercises.instructions: Choose the detail from Chapter 6 that supports Chapter 7.
exercises.question: Chapter 7 says, “They made a mistake, but it wasn’t on purpose.” Which detail from Chapter 6 supports this?
options: Iblis tricked them, and they forgot Allah’s warning.
Allah had never told them about the forbidden tree.
Eve picked the fruit first and gave it to Adam.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6 says: “He convinced them to believe his lies, and they forgot the warning Allah had given them.” The warning itself was clear: “Allah only asked them not to go near one tree.” And it was Adam who “offered it to Eve”.

feedback.correct: Yes. They were tricked and they forgot; they did not choose to disobey Allah.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 6. What happened to Allah’s warning before they ate?

exercises.title: Adam’s Path
exercises.instructions: Put these stages of Adam’s life in order.
exercises.question: How does Adam’s life move from creation to his legacy?

sequencingItems.text: Adam and Eve are pardoned and put on earth to live there.
Adam’s children and grandchildren spread his message worldwide.
Allah gives Adam life and intellect to learn and understand.
When a community forms, Adam becomes the first Messenger of Allah.
Adam starts to feel lonely in Paradise, and Allah gives him Eve.
On earth, Adam and Eve struggle to survive and work hard.

exercises.explanation: Life and intellect (Chapter 2), Eve in Paradise (Chapter 5), pardon and life on earth (Chapter 7), the struggle to survive (Chapter 8), and then: “when a community formed, Adam (pbuh) became the first Messenger of Allah” (Chapter 9). Finally, his children and grandchildren “spread his message worldwide” (Chapter 12).

feedback.correct: Yes. Adam became a Messenger only after years on earth, and his message lived on after him.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Adam became a Messenger on earth, “after a period of time”, not in Paradise.

exercises.title: Cause and Result
exercises.instructions: Match each cause with its result.
exercises.question: What did each of these lead to?

matchingPairs.left: Adam started to feel lonely in Paradise.
matchingPairs.right: Allah gave him Eve to be his companion.

matchingPairs.left: Adam and Eve forgot Allah’s warning.
matchingPairs.right: They both ate from the forbidden tree.
Adam became the first Messenger of Allah.
Allah accepted his offering.

Allah gave him Eve to be his companion.
They both ate from the forbidden tree.
Adam became the first Messenger of Allah.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: Adam “started to feel lonely”, so “Allah gave him a wife called Eve (Hawwa) to be his companion.” Chapter 6: “they forgot the warning Allah had given them” and “They both ate of the forbidden tree.” Chapter 9: “when a community formed, Adam (pbuh) became the first Messenger of Allah.” Chapter 11: “Allah accepted Habil’s offering because he gave from his heart.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Each event in the story leads to the next one, in good ways and in bad ways.
feedback.incorrect: Look for “so”, “because” and “when” in Chapters 5, 6, 9 and 11.

exercises.title: After the Crime
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: Qabil felt no regret at all after he killed his brother.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 says: “Soon, Qabil’s anger cooled, and he felt very sad. He also started to panic.” He said, “I killed my brother. I did the worst thing in life.”

feedback.correct: Right. When his anger cooled, Qabil understood what he had done and felt very sad.
feedback.incorrect: Read what happened to Qabil when his anger cooled in Chapter 11. What did he feel and say?

exercises.title: Two Sons in One Day
exercises.instructions: Choose the explanation the story supports.
exercises.question: Only Habil was killed. Why does Chapter 12 say Adam “lost both of his sons on the same day”?
options: Both sons were killed in the same fight.
Habil died, and Qabil went far away.
Both sons left to live in other lands.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12 begins: “He went far away. Prophet Adam (pbuh) became very sad. He lost both of his sons on the same day.” Adam lost Habil through death and Qabil because he went away.

feedback.correct: Yes. One son died, and the other son left after the crime, so Adam lost both of them.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first three sentences of Chapter 12. What happened to the son who was still alive?

exercises.title: The Lesson for Believers
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 12 with one word: jealousy, work or people.
exercises.question: What lesson does the story give true believers?
exercises.fillBlanksText: The story suggests that true believers should stay away from [blank] and control their anger.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12 says: “The story suggests that true believers should stay away from jealousy and control their anger.” In Chapter 10, “Qabil was mostly jealous”, and later his “face became very dark with anger”.

feedback.correct: Yes. Qabil’s jealousy and anger led to the first crime, so the lesson is to control both.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first lines of Chapter 12. Which feeling did Qabil have in Chapter 10?
